date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Moses, called "the man of God," blessed the children of Israel before his death (Deut 33:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:1, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording "the man of God"); JFB on Deut 33:1 ("a common designation of a prophet," applied as Moses delivered "a prophetic benediction").

claims.claim: The blessing opens with a theophany: the LORD came from Sinai, rose from Seir, shone from Paran, with ten thousands of saints (Deut 33:2–3).
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 33:2 (one appearance at Sinai, glory spreading like sunrise); K&D reads "ten thousands of saints" as "out of holy myriads," the holy angels surrounding God's throne (1 Kgs 22:19; Dan 7:10; Ps 89:6).

claims.claim: "From his right hand went a fiery law for them" (33:2, KJV) rests on the two-word reading dāth ʾēsh; the one-word reading ʾeshdāth, "shooting fire" (lightning), is very probable but not established.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:2, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on Deut 33:2, read in full (the two-word reading "fails to give a suitable sense"; dāth is Persian loanword, used of God's law only by Gentiles, Ezra 7:12; Dan 6:6; cf. Hab 3:4).

claims.claim: "He was king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people and the tribes of Israel were gathered together" (33:5) — whether "king" is the LORD's kingship or the beginning of human monarchy is unclear.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:5, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on Deut 33:2–5 (the LORD "became King of Israel" at Sinai).

claims.claim: Reuben is blessed for survival, not pre-eminence: "Let Reuben live, and not die; and let not his men be few" (33:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording "Let Reuben live, and not die; and let not his men be few"); JFB on Deut 33:6 (deprived of primogeniture, "still to hold rank as one of the tribes"; "gradually he sank into a mere nomadic tribe").

claims.claim: Simeon is named nowhere in Deuteronomy 33; eleven tribes are blessed by name.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:6–25, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, Asher; no Simeon).

claims.claim: No explanation for Simeon's omission is established; the leading proposals are Jacob's unrevoked curse (Gen 49:5–7), absorption into Judah's lot (Josh 19:1), and a textual loss.
claims.evidence: Gen 49:5–7; Matthew Henry on Deut 33 (read in part via search excerpt: Jacob's brand, diminution, Zimri of Peor); Wesley's notes on Deut 33:6 (read in part: curse or absorption into Judah); BibleHub 33:6 commentary (read in part: Rashi's absorption view).

claims.claim: Some Septuagint manuscripts insert Simeon in Deut 33:6 ("let Simeon be many in number" / "let the men of Simeon be many"); the Masoretic text omits Simeon.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 33:6, read in full ("Many eminent biblical scholars, resting on the most ancient and approved manuscripts of the Septuagint, consider the latter clause as referring to Simeon"); BibleHub 33:6 commentary (Alexandrian MS reading, read in part); Josephus, Ant. 4.8.48 n.1 (Simeon "not omitted in his copy, as it unhappily now is, both in our Hebrew and Samaritan copies").

claims.claim: Judah's blessing prays for his hearing, his return to his people, sufficient hands, and help against enemies (33:7).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 33:7 ("great power and independence of Judah… taking the lead in all military expeditions").

claims.claim: Levi is given the Thummim and the Urim, as the "holy one" proved at Massah and striven with at Meribah (33:8).
claims.evidence: BDB H224 ʾūrîm, read in full ("thy Thummim and thy Urim [is] the man of thy favour, i.e. the Levite tested at Massah & Meribah").

claims.claim: The physical form of the Urim and Thummim and the mechanism by which they gave answers are not established; Scripture gives little information.
claims.evidence: BDB H224, read in full ("These passages give little information"; records Josephus' shining-gems view, Philo's two-images view, and the sacred-lot view without settling the mechanism).

claims.claim: Levi's loyalty "unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him" (33:9) most probably refers to the Levites' severity after the golden calf (Ex 32:27–29).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 33:8–10, read in full ("their unsparing severity in chastising even their nearest and dearest relatives who had participated in the idolatry of the molten calf, Ex 32:25–28"). The text itself names no event.

claims.claim: Levi's appointed functions are teaching Jacob God's judgments and Israel his law, putting incense before God, and whole burnt sacrifice on the altar (33:10).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 33:8–10 (the Levites' appointment "to the dignified and sacred office of the priesthood," Lev 10:11; Deut 17:8–11).

claims.claim: Benjamin, "the beloved of the Lord," dwells in safety by him and "between his shoulders" (33:12); the temple-border reading (Moriah in Benjamin's confines) is the probable referent.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:12, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (wording per KJV — the unaffected "between his shoulders" clause only; see clm-deu-10-041 for the stored-text error); JFB on Deut 33:12, read in full ("Mount Moriah, the site of the sacred edifice, lay in the confines of Benjamin"). The text names no temple.

claims.claim: Joseph receives the longest tribal blessing (33:13–17): the precious things of heaven, dew, the deep, sun, moon, ancient mountains, lasting hills, earth, and the good will of him that dwelt in the bush.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 33:13–17 (territory "diversified by hill and dale, wood and water… rich in all the productions").

claims.claim: Joseph's blessing names both Joseph tribes: "they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh" (33:17).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording "they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh"); JFB on Deut 33:13–17 (the bullock's horns "shadowed forth the triumphs of Joshua and the new kingdom of Jeroboam, both of whom were of Ephraim").

claims.claim: Zebulun and Issachar share a blessing of sea-going trade and hidden treasures: "they shall suck of the abundance of the seas, and of treasures hid in the sand" (33:18–19), probably the Phoenician trade in murex dye and Belus glass.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:18–19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 33:18–19, read in full (Zebulun "on commercial enterprises and voyages by sea"; murex and glass from the river Belus). The text names no commodity.

claims.claim: Gad, enlarged and lion-like, took the first portion east of Jordan and kept faith by joining the invasion (33:20–21).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 33:20–21 ("settled by Moses himself in the first portion of land conquered… they faithfully kept their engagement to join the 'heads of the people' in the invasion of Canaan").

claims.claim: Dan "is a lion's whelp: he shall leap from Bashan" (33:22), probably the Danite migration to the northern colony at Laish (Judg 18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:22, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on Deut 33:22, read in full ("by a sudden and successful irruption, established a colony in the northern extremity of the land… the leap of a young lion from the hills of Bashan"). The text names no migration.

claims.claim: Naphtali is "satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the Lord," to possess the west and the south (33:23).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:23, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording "satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the Lord"); JFB on Deut 33:23 (territory "to 'the west,' on the borders of lakes Merom and Chinnereth, and to 'the south' of the northern Danites").

claims.claim: Asher is blessed with children, acceptance, feet dipped in oil, shoes of iron and brass, and strength as his days (33:24–25), probably his olive-rich coastal land.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 33:24–25, read in full ("his district as particularly fertile and adapted to the culture of the olive"; iron/brass shoes "suited his rocky coast from Carmel to Sidon").

claims.claim: The blessing closes with a theophany frame: "There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun… The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms" (33:26–29).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 33:26–29, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording "There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun… The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms"); JFB on Deut 33:26–29 ("a congratulatory address to Israel on their peculiar happiness and privilege in having Jehovah for their God and protector").

claims.claim: The Blessing of Moses is archaic poetry resembling Gen 49 and Judg 5; whether it dates to the early premonarchic period is debated — its archaic character is observed, its date is not established.
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 33, read in full (the Moses blessing confirms and reworks the Blessing of Jacob, Gen 49; "not the slightest trace of the historical circumstances… peculiar to the post-Mosaic times"; the speaker "must have lived in a time preceding the prophetic age").

claims.claim: The blessing was pronounced by Moses, not written down by him like the song of ch. 32; the heading (33:1) and the introductory formulas ("and this for Judah," "and to Levi he said," etc.) are an editor's additions, and the arrangement is probably the editor's work.
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 33, read in full ("This blessing was not written down by Moses himself, like the song in ch. 32, but simply pronounced in the presence of the assembled tribes… the editor clearly distinguishes himself from Moses, by speaking of Moses as 'the man of God'"). A scholarly judgment about composition, not a textual fact.

claims.claim: The Blessing of Moses confirms and reworks the Blessing of Jacob (Gen 49): same dying-blessing form, same Joseph prominence, Levi's curse turned to blessing, Simeon dropped.
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 33, read in full (the Moses blessing "would contain simply a confirmation of that of the dying patriarch, and would be founded upon it in various ways"; "not surpassed in independence and originality by that of Jacob").

claims.claim: Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, over against Jericho (34:1).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 34:1 ("the head or summit of the Pisgah… The general name given to the whole mountain range east of Jordan, was Abarim").

claims.claim: The LORD showed Moses all the land from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah to the utmost sea, the south, and the Jericho plain to Zoar (34:1–3); whether this was natural sight, divinely aided sight, or a description of extent is debated — the Mediterranean, Dan, and Zoar lie beyond ordinary sight from Nebo.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 34:1, read in full (no miraculous power of vision; "any man could do [it], if he attained sufficient elevation"); K&D on Deut 34:1 (read in part via search excerpt: "a sight with the bodily eyes, whose natural power of vision was miraculously increased by God"); BiblicalTraining, "Mount Nebo," read in full (Mediterranean hidden, Dan and Zoar beyond ordinary sight; divine showing and description-of-extent "are compatible").

claims.claim: "Unto Dan" (34:1) may name Laish-Dan, renamed after Moses' death (Judg 18:27–29), or a Dan in northern Peraea not yet discovered; neither identification is established.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:1, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on Deut 34:1 (read in part: "not Laish-Dan near the central source of the Jordan (Jdg 18:27), which did not belong to Gilead, but a Dan in northern Peraea, which has not yet been discovered"); Wesley's notes on Deut 34:1 (read in part: "Unto Dan — To that city, which after Moses's death was called so").

claims.claim: The LORD named the land shown to Moses as the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which Moses might see with his eyes but not enter (34:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Moses died in the land of Moab at 120 years old, his eye not dim and his natural force unabated (34:5, 7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:5, 7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); cf. Deut 31:2 ("I am an hundred and twenty years old this day").

claims.claim: God buried Moses in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day" (34:6) — the grave is unknown by the text's own statement.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (for the quoted wording "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day"); JFB on Deut 34:6 ("This concealment seems to have been owing to a special and wise arrangement of Providence, to prevent its being ranked among 'holy places'").

claims.claim: Later tradition holds Moses was buried by angels (Jude 9) or by immortal powers (Philo); the biblical text names no agent but God ("he buried him").
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) ("he buried him"); JFB on Deut 34:6, read in full ("according to an ancient tradition of Jews and Christians, buried by angels (Jude 9)"); Philo, De vita Mosis II.291 (read in part: "entombed not by mortal hands, but by immortal powers").

claims.claim: Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, and the days of mourning were ended (34:8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Thirty days (rather than the usual seven) marks mourning for a person of high rank or official eminence.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 34:8, read in full ("Seven days was the usual period of mourning, but for persons in high rank or official eminence, it was extended to thirty (Gen 50:3–10; Num 20:29)"). A commentary reading of the custom.

claims.claim: Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him, and Israel hearkened to him (34:9).
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 34:9 ("appointed to a peculiar and extraordinary office… the general or leader, called to head the people in the war of invasion").

claims.claim: Deuteronomy 34 was written subsequently to Moses' death — its third-person, retrospective standpoint ("unto this day," "there arose not a prophet since") implies a later hand; whether Joshua, Eleazar, Samuel, Ezra, or another is debated.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 34:5–10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) (retrospective standpoint); JFB on Deut 34:1, read in full ("appears from internal evidence to have been written subsequently to the death of Moses, and it probably formed, at one time, an introduction to the Book of Joshua"); Talmud, Bava Batra 14b–15a (Joshua wrote the last eight verses) — second-hand via the BibleHub article and the Curley paper excerpt (see §12.4); the Joshua attribution is Traditional, the later-hand standpoint is Probable.

claims.claim: The traditional Nebo ridge (Jebel en-Neba / Ras es-Siyagha, ~10 km northwest of Madaba) is the strongest candidate for Mount Nebo: the name Neba survives almost unchanged, and the biblical fixed points (Abarim range, above the plains of Moab, across from Jericho, broad western view) fit.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Mount Nebo," read in full ("The survival of the name Neba makes this ridge the strongest candidate, and it is the identification most scholars accept"); HISTORICAL-GEOGRAPHY-REPORT.md (workspace provisional: "Recognizable traditional geographical association").

claims.claim: The precise viewing point and the burial spot on Nebo are unknown — no evidence identifies them, and Deut 34:6 explicitly leaves the grave unknown.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Mount Nebo," read in full ("The precise summit is still debated"); HISTORICAL-GEOGRAPHY-REPORT.md ("Moses' death or burial spot unverified").

claims.claim: 2 Maccabees 2:4–8 tells that Jeremiah hid the ark, tabernacle, and altar of incense in a cave on the mountain from which Moses viewed the land; the story has no support in the biblical books and no such cave has been found.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Mount Nebo," read in full (2 Macc 2:4–8 summary; "no support in the biblical books, and no such cave has been found"). 2 Maccabees is not part of the Protestant canon.

claims.claim: There is no direct archaeological evidence for Moses' viewing of the land, his death, or his burial.
claims.evidence: §6.2 — the negative fact, stated as such. The excavated remains on the Nebo ridge are Byzantine (4th c. church and monastery on Ras es-Siyagha) and later; no second-millennium inscription, tomb, or artefact is tied to Deut 34.

claims.claim: The stored Preview KJV text of Deut 33:12 reads "the Lord shall cover him," but the KJV reads "the LORD shall cover him" (YHWH) — a substantive stored-text error in this category.
claims.evidence: Dev 1 KJV check report, KJV-DEUTERONOMY-1-34-VERIFICATION-20261120.md, read in full in this session (Class A error, confirmed raw from the saved API JSON and against BibleHub + Blue Letter Bible; same class as the Numbers errors Num 14:17, 31:28). The stored Preview text of Deut 33:12 reads "the Lord" where the KJV reads "the LORD" (YHWH). Yonatan DECIDED 2026-11-20 ~07:21 AM CST to LEAVE the stored text as-is as an accepted known limitation (Option A re-grounding; no hosted-DB write — the ~11:58 PM 2026-11-19 FIX decision is superseded). The KJV source for Deuteronomy therefore stays NOT-INDEPENDENTLY-VERIFIED and is no longer cited by this category.

connections.note: The Blessing of Moses confirms and reworks the Blessing of Jacob: same dying-blessing form, same Joseph prominence, Levi's curse turned to blessing, Simeon dropped.
The Sinai/Seir theophany march recurs in the Song of Deborah (K&D on 33:2).
"God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran" — the same theophany geography (K&D on 33:2).
"O God, when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst march through the wilderness… the earth shook, the heavens also dropped at the presence of God: even Sinai itself."
The institution of the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece of judgment, which Levi is given custody of (BDB H224).
Eleazar inquires for Joshua "after the judgment of Urim" — the Urim's function for the incoming leader (BDB H224).
The Levites' severity after the golden calf, the probable referent of Levi's loyalty "unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him" (JFB).
The Levites "shall teach Jacob thy judgments" — the teaching office (Lev 10:11; JFB).
Joseph's blessing in both dying blessings: fruitful bough, blessings of heaven and the deep, the head of him separated from his brethren.
Ephraim's greatness over Manasseh ("his younger brother shall be greater than he") behind "the ten thousands of Ephraim, and… the thousands of Manasseh."
"Jeshurun" — the poetic name for Israel, waxed fat and kicked (32:15); the king in Jeshurun (33:5) is the same people's God.
The command to ascend Nebo on the very day Moses finished the song: "Get thee up into this mountain Abarim, unto mount Nebo… and behold the land of Canaan."
The earlier command: "Get thee up into this mount Abarim, and see the land which I have given unto the children of Israel."
Moses' plea to cross over and see the good land, refused; told to climb Pisgah, look, and commission Joshua — answered in 34:1–4.
The land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: "Unto thy seed will I give this land" (Gen 12:7), restated in Deut 34:4.
The reason Moses dies outside the land: "Because ye believed me not… ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them" (cf. Deut 32:51–52).

"Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses" — the New Testament allusion to the tradition around the unknown burial (Origen attributes it to the lost ending of the Assumption of Moses; the surviving text breaks off before Moses' death).
Moses appears with Elijah at the Transfiguration — the man whose burial place is unknown is seen alive with the Lord (cf. Deane on Jude 9).
"I am an hundred and twenty years old this day" (31:2) — the age restated at the death (34:7).
Thirty days of mourning for Aaron (Num 20:29) — the same honour given to Moses (JFB on 34:8).
The laying on of hands: Moses lays his hands on Joshua, gives him charge, and puts of his honour upon him "that all the congregation… may be obedient."
"After the death of Moses the servant of the Lord it came to pass, that the Lord spake unto Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' minister" — the transition Deut 34:9 opens.

"The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me" — the promise against which 34:10's "there arose not a prophet since… like unto Moses" is measured.
Peter cites Deut 18:15–19 ("A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me") as fulfilled in Christ.
"Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after" — the epitaph's "servant of the Lord" (34:5) in the New Testament's reading.
Pisgah as a border landmark ("the plain… under Ashdoth-pisgah") — the mountain's place in the land's geography.
